When we finally went enterprise, my VP of Sales told me he wanted to bring his laptop along to every single prospect call and meeting. I asked why. He said so he could show off the product right then and there. So it would be easier to close the sale. Well, sure. Of course. But he also knew something important. In bigger enterprises, you don’t always win.

answer: The truth is that most candidates are terrible at interviews. Not because they’re stupid or unqualified — it’s just that nobody practices anymore. I know you’ve been told this before. But let me tell you why it matters more than ever today and how you can actually stand out by being different. Why Interviews Have Changed (And Why This Matters More Than Ever) The days when an interview was as simple as showing up with your resume and answering basic questions? Those days are gone. Gone for good. Today, every candidate looks exactly the same on paper : – Studied CS50 on Harvard Extension Website – Had 2 years experience working remotely from home – “Able to work effectively in a team environment” – “Strong communication skills” What makes one person truly special over another? That’s what everyone wants to know. And if you want to get hired, especially these days … you have to show them. Why Most Candidates Fail Let’s break down what happens in most interviews. They go like this: Candidate walks in, sits down, fumbles through their notes, tries to remember the company name… and then launches into something generic about how excited they are to be there, learn new things, meet great people, etc. Then they launch into whatever rehearsed answers they practiced with a recruiter, maybe mentioning a few buzzwords here and there. Maybe they even pretend to understand some industry jargon that sounds impressive but means nothing specific. Sound familiar? It should. Because almost everyone does this. The thing is, this approach doesn’t reveal anything unique about YOU. All it shows is that you followed the standard playbook without putting any thought into who you really are, what you bring to the table, or how you’d specifically crush it at this role.

answer: Dear SaaStr: What are some tactics you’d recommend for retaining angry customers? You know, those folks that are threatening to cancel their contract. First, understand there’s only so much you can do here. If they have no value at all from your product, and it doesn’t work … well, then maybe you’ll just lose them anyway. But if they use your app, but aren’t getting enough ROI or value — you might be able to save these folks. And often, later on, this will make them advocates for life. The best way to handle a potential churner is by not letting things get to that point. That means being proactive before they even think about leaving. Here are my top suggestions to prevent churn (and/or save a potentially lost customer): #1. Get on the phone with the CEO / Founder ASAP. Your CRO may want to take over any issues, as may support. It may seem like an efficient use of time to route it through someone else. But I’ve almost never seen this help. Instead, jump on the phone yourself. Tell the customer you’re sorry. Ask why they’re mad. Be honest and transparent. Share data. Show them the roadmap. Get them involved in the future. This usually helps de-escalate things, and build trust. Even if it’s too late to retain them immediately, it gets them back on the team’s radar, which matters.

So many founders that are struggling to hit their numbers, growing slower than planned … and then they run out of cash anyway. Because even though they aren’t growing fast enough or hitting their plan, at least they’re not burning much. And they don’t realize until it’s almost too late how far behind they really are. How do you avoid running out of money when things get tougher? A few thoughts: First, if you have any sort of traction (even just one customer), hire someone full-time to manage your finances. This will force everyone to focus on efficiency. What actually works well: One great thing we did at Adobe Sign / EchoSign was build a “Zero Cash” slide into our monthly board meeting deck.
